justification: Minimal pigment oculocutaneous albinism type 1 (OCA1B/OCA1-MP) is a well-defined autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in the nuclear TYR (tyrosinase) gene, with residual enzyme activity accounting for the minimal pigment phenotype. MT-TG encodes the mitochondrial tRNA for glycine and its reported pathogenic variants are linked to mitochondrial syndromes such as cardiomyopathy, encephalomyopathy, MELAS/MERRF-like presentations, and rare optic/retinal involvement—none of which include albinism or melanin biosynthesis defects. There is no known mechanistic pathway connecting mitochondrial tRNA-Gly function to melanosomal tyrosinase activity, and no human genetic studies implicate MT-TG in any form of oculocutaneous albinism. Any co-mention in the literature would be incidental (e.g., broad mitochondrial or ophthalmic gene panels). Therefore the relationship is best classified as Novel, with only trivial residual probability for a speculative biological rationale.

Autosomal dominant hypocalcemia type 1 is well established to be caused by gain-of-function variants in CASR (the calcium-sensing receptor), with ADH2 caused by GNA11; there is no recognized role for KREMEN1 in this disorder. KREMEN1 encodes a Dickkopf co-receptor that modulates Wnt/β-catenin signaling and its human disease association is with autosomal recessive ectodermal dysplasia (hair/tooth type), not calcium homeostasis or parathyroid function. At most, one could construct an indirect biological rationale via Wnt signaling in bone and mineral metabolism, which supports a small allocation to "Hypothesized," but this is speculative and not phenotype-specific. No human genetic studies link KREMEN1 variants to hypocalcemia or PTH dysregulation, so the relationship appears essentially novel/incidental.

phenotype: congenital stationary night blindness autosomal dominant 3
justification: TFRC (transferrin receptor 1) is established as the disease gene for combined immunodeficiency (IMD46) due to biallelic variants affecting receptor internalization, and it has no reported role in inherited retinal disease. Congenital stationary night blindness, autosomal dominant type 3 (CSNBAD3) is attributed to GNAT1 variants, with other dominant CSNB forms caused by RHO and PDE6B; TFRC is not among candidate or reported CSNB genes. A weak biological rationale exists because iron uptake via transferrin receptor is relevant to retinal pigment epithelium and photoreceptor metabolism, and iron dysregulation can cause retinal degeneration, which supports a small allocation to Hypothesized. However, there are no human genetic reports, functional retinal disease models, or linkage data connecting TFRC to CSNBAD3, so the relationship is best classified as Novel.

ADPKD is caused predominantly by PKD1 and PKD2, with additional minor/atypical genes including GANAB, DNAJB11, ALG9, ALG5, IFT140 and NEK8-related cystic disease; POU4F1 (BRN3A) is not among any reported ADPKD or polycystic kidney gene panels. POU4F1 is a POU-domain (class IV) transcription factor best characterized in sensory neuron and neuroblastoma biology, with no established role in renal tubular epithelial differentiation, ciliary function, or cystogenesis. I am unaware of any human genetic study, family segregation, or association analysis implicating POU4F1 variants in ADPKD or in recognized precursor phenotypes. A small probability is retained for "hypothesized" given that POU-family transcription factors can be broadly expressed in kidney and could be mentioned in transcriptomic profiling of cystic tissue, which would provide weak biological rationale. Overall, the evidence strongly favors a novel (no evidence) classification.

Mitochondrial pyruvate carrier deficiency is a rare autosomal recessive metabolic disorder caused by biallelic variants in MPC1 (BRP44L), with MPC2 occasionally implicated; BRSK2 is not among the recognized disease genes. BRSK2 (SAD-A kinase) is established as a cause of a neurodevelopmental disorder with autism, intellectual disability and hypotonia, but no reported patients with lactate/pyruvate elevation attributable to carrier deficiency. A weak, indirect biological rationale exists because BRSK2 is an AMPK-related, LKB1-regulated kinase implicated in cellular energy sensing and insulin secretion, which could conceivably intersect with pyruvate metabolism, supporting a small "Hypothesized" allocation. However, there is no human genetic or direct functional evidence linking BRSK2 variants to MPC deficiency, so the relationship is best classified as novel.

Antley-Bixler syndrome is genetically well characterized, caused by gain-of-function FGFR2 variants (craniosynostosis-predominant form) and by biallelic POR (cytochrome P450 oxidoreductase) variants (form with disordered steroidogenesis). C1QBP (p32/gC1qR, 17p13.3) is instead associated with autosomal recessive combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency 33, presenting as mitochondrial cardiomyopathy, myopathy and lactic acidosis, with no reported skeletal/craniofacial dysostosis resembling Antley-Bixler. I am not aware of any human genetic study, case report, or functional work implicating C1QBP variants in Antley-Bixler syndrome or in POR/FGFR2 pathways. A small residual probability is allotted to "hypothesized" because C1QBP's mitochondrial and complement/ signaling roles could theoretically be invoked in generic developmental or steroidogenic contexts, but this would be speculative pathway-level reasoning rather than evidence.

phenotype: metabolic encephalomyopathic crises, recurrent, with rhabdomyolysis, cardiac arrhythmias, and neurodegeneration
justification: Recurrent metabolic encephalomyopathic crises with rhabdomyolysis, cardiac arrhythmias, and neurodegeneration (MIM 616878) is a well-defined recessive disorder caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in TANGO2 at 22q11.21; no TRHR variants have been implicated in this condition. TRHR (8q23) encodes the thyrotropin-releasing hormone receptor, and its known human phenotype is generalized TRH resistance with central hypothyroidism, a clinically and mechanistically distinct disease. A tenuous biological link could be argued because thyroid hormone deficiency can predispose to myopathy/rhabdomyolysis and cardiac conduction changes, which might justify a small allocation to Hypothesized, but there is no literature connecting TRHR to this specific crisis-driven encephalomyopathy. Any co-mention would be incidental (e.g., differential diagnosis lists or broad gene panels), supporting a Novel classification.

phenotype: spinal muscular atrophy-progressive myoclonic epilepsy syndrome
justification: Spinal muscular atrophy with progressive myoclonic epilepsy (SMA-PME) is well established as an autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic ASAH1 mutations, with rare additional reports implicating other genes (e.g., ASAH1-negative cases occasionally attributed to other loci); KIF17 is not among the recognized causal genes. KIF17 is a kinesin-2 family motor protein involved in dendritic/intraflagellar transport (e.g., NMDA receptor NR2B trafficking, ciliary transport), and while other kinesins (KIF5A, KIF1A, KIF1B) cause motor neuron and neurodegenerative disease, this provides only generic biological plausibility rather than direct evidence. Most such KIF17 functional data derive from mouse and in vitro systems, which would support at most a "Hypothesized" designation. I am unaware of any human genetic study reporting KIF17 variants in SMA-PME probands, so the weight falls predominantly on Novel with a modest allowance for undiscovered candidate-gene or exome reports.

Hemochromatosis type 1 is a well-defined monogenic disorder caused by variants in HFE (chromosome 6p22), with p.C282Y and p.H63D as the principal alleles; modifier effects are attributed to genes in iron metabolism pathways such as HAMP, HFE2/HJV, TFR2, SLC40A1, and BMP/SMAD signaling components. CEP120 encodes a centriolar/centrosomal protein required for centriole elongation and ciliogenesis, and its disease associations in humans are ciliopathies (Joubert syndrome with associated features, short-rib thoracic dysplasia/Jeune asphyxiating thoracic dystrophy). I am unaware of any human genetic study, GWAS of iron indices, or functional work linking CEP120 variants or expression to iron overload or HFE-related hemochromatosis. There is no obvious mechanistic pathway connecting centriole biology to hepcidin regulation or intestinal iron absorption, so even a "hypothesized" designation lacks support. Accordingly, the evidence overwhelmingly favors a Novel classification, with only minimal probability reserved for obscure or incidental reports.

GHR encodes the growth hormone receptor and is not among the recognized congenital long QT syndrome genes (KCNQ1, KCNH2, SCN5A, KCNE1/2, CACNA1C, CALM1-3, etc.), and it does not appear in ClinGen/expert-curated LQTS gene panels or curation efforts. There is no credible report of GHR variants segregating with or being associated with familial LQTS in probands or families. Some indirect biological rationale exists: growth hormone excess (acromegaly) and GH deficiency have been linked to altered ventricular repolarization and QTc/QT dispersion changes in humans, and GH/IGF-1 signaling modulates cardiomyocyte ion channel expression and hypertrophy, which could support a weak "hypothesized" pathway link—but these concern acquired repolarization changes, not inherited LQTS. Therefore most weight belongs in Novel, with a modest allocation to Hypothesized for the endocrine–repolarization biology, and only minimal probability for Existing/Established.

GYPC encodes glycophorin C, an erythrocyte membrane sialoglycoprotein defining the Gerbich blood group, with established disease associations limited to Gerbich-negative/Leach phenotypes, hereditary elliptocytosis, and modulation of Plasmodium falciparum (EBA-140) invasion. Neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis type 6B (Kufs type A, adult-onset) is caused by biallelic variants in CLN6, a gene on 15q23 encoding an ER membrane protein, with no reported role for GYPC. There are no human genetic, functional, or lysosomal-pathway data implicating GYPC in NCL pathogenesis, and GYPC expression is largely restricted to erythroid tissue rather than neurons or lysosomes. Any co-mention in the literature would be incidental (e.g., large sequencing panels or gene lists). Therefore the relationship is best classified as Novel, with a small allowance for unrecognized biological speculation.

CYBA encodes p22phox, an essential subunit of NADPH oxidases, and its common variants (e.g., C242T, A640G) have been studied mainly in cardiovascular, renal, diabetic and some general cancer-risk contexts, not in parathyroid neoplasia. The established genetics of parathyroid carcinoma centers on CDC73/HRPT2 (germline and somatic), with additional contributions from CCND1, PRUNE2, and the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway; CYBA is not among reported drivers or susceptibility loci. A plausible but indirect biological rationale exists—NADPH oxidase–derived reactive oxygen species contribute to oxidative stress, proliferation and tumorigenesis, and oxidative stress has been described in hyperparathyroidism—so a "hypothesized" link cannot be fully excluded. However, I am not aware of any human genetic association study specifically testing CYBA variants in parathyroid carcinoma or its recognized precursors, so most weight falls on Novel with some on Hypothesized.

phenotype: aldosterone-producing adenoma with seizures and neurological abnormalities
justification: The syndrome of primary aldosteronism with seizures and neurological abnormalities (PASNA/ASNA) is a well-defined channelopathy caused by de novo gain-of-function variants in CACNA1D, with somatic KCNJ5, ATP1A1, ATP2B3, CACNA1H and CTNNB1 variants underlying other forms of aldosterone-producing adenoma; SLC25A13 has no reported role in this entity. SLC25A13 encodes citrin, the mitochondrial aspartate–glutamate carrier, and its biallelic variants cause NICCD, failure to thrive/dyslipidemia, and adult-onset citrullinemia type II with encephalopathy and occasionally seizures—this partial neurological overlap provides only a weak, nonspecific biological rationale (hence some weight to Hypothesized). There is no evidence linking citrin deficiency to adrenal zona glomerulosa function, calcium signaling in aldosterone-producing cells, or adenoma formation. Any co-mention in the literature would be incidental, e.g., through broad metabolic or mitochondrial gene panels. Therefore the relationship is best characterized as Novel, with a modest allowance for a hypothesized mitochondrial/neurometabolic link.

phenotype: polycystic lipomembranous osteodysplasia with sclerosing leukoencephalopathy 1
justification: Polycystic lipomembranous osteodysplasia with sclerosing leukoencephalopathy type 1 (Nasu-Hakola disease, PLOSL1) is well established to result from biallelic loss-of-function variants in TYROBP (DAP12), with PLOSL2 caused by TREM2; GGPS1 is not among the recognized disease genes. GGPS1 variants have instead been reported in an autosomal recessive muscular dystrophy with hearing loss and ovarian insufficiency, and GGPS1 is known in bone biology as a downstream target of nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates affecting osteoclast prenylation, which provides only a loose, indirect mechanistic rationale for bone-cyst phenotypes. I am unaware of any human genetic study implicating GGPS1 variants in PLOSL1 probands or families. Therefore most weight goes to Novel, with a moderate allocation to Hypothesized based on plausible osteoclast/prenylation pathway relevance, and only minimal probability for Existing or Established.

Striate palmoplantar keratoderma is a well-characterized desmosomal disorder caused by variants in DSG1 (PPKS1), DSP (PPKS2), and KRT1 (PPKS3); TCF3 is not among the recognized disease genes in OMIM/GenCC for this phenotype. TCF3 (E2A) is best known in humans for autosomal dominant and recessive agammaglobulinemia and B-cell development defects, with no reported palmoplantar keratoderma phenotype. Some biological plausibility exists because the mouse "Tcf3" literature (largely referring to Tcf7l1, a Wnt pathway factor) implicates it in epidermal and hair follicle stem cell fate, and E-proteins/Id factors modulate keratinocyte differentiation — this supports a modest allocation to Hypothesized, though such evidence is non-human and indirect. I therefore concentrate probability on Novel with a substantial secondary weight on Hypothesized, and only small weight on Existing/Established in case of an unfamiliar single-case report.

phenotype: developmental delay, hypotonia, and impaired language
justification: Biallelic PCBD1 variants cause pterin-4a-carbinolamine dehydratase deficiency, a BH4-related hyperphenylalaninemia (primapterinuria) documented in multiple human patients, and later also MODY5-like diabetes and hypomagnesemia. Human case series (e.g., Thönnes et al.) report largely benign outcomes with normal cognitive development, but individual patients have shown transient neurological signs including hypotonia, delayed motor milestones and mild developmental/speech delay, so limited human evidence links the gene to this phenotype. Moreover, the underlying mechanism—BH4 cofactor deficiency with hyperphenylalaninemia and potential monoamine neurotransmitter disturbance—is a well-recognized precursor of developmental delay and hypotonia, supporting "Existing." Evidence is not replicated or consistent enough across independent probands to call the specific triad "Established," since most reported patients are neurologically normal. A residual probability is retained for "Hypothesized," reflecting that much of the neurodevelopmental rationale is mechanistic/pathway-based rather than directly phenotype-proven.

The genes with credible human genetic evidence in Fuchs' endothelial corneal dystrophy are COL8A2, SLC4A11, ZEB1/TCF8, TCF4 (CTG18.1 repeat expansion), AGBL1, LOXHD1, and GWAS loci KANK4, LAMC1 and ATP1B1; IFNAR2 (21q22.11) is not among the recognized loci in any replicated linkage, GWAS, or sequencing study I am aware of. Thus "Established" is essentially excluded and "Existing" is unlikely, though a modest allowance remains for an unreplicated association in a newer or multiethnic GWAS/candidate study that I may not recall. There is a plausible biological rationale, since expanded CUG repeat RNA in TCF4-associated FECD and other stress responses in corneal endothelium have been linked to innate immune/type I interferon pathway activation, in which IFNAR2 is a core receptor subunit—supporting some weight for "Hypothesized." Overall, the balance of my knowledge favors no direct genetic evidence, with a pathway-level rather than variant-level connection.

TCTN1 (tectonic family member 1) encodes a transition-zone ciliary protein; biallelic variants are established causes of ciliopathies such as Joubert syndrome (JBTS13) and Meckel-type phenotypes, with no reported role in cytosolic glycan catabolism. Congenital disorder of deglycosylation type 2 is attributed to biallelic MAN2C1 variants (with CDDG1 due to NGLY1), pathways involving cytosolic deglycosylation/free oligosaccharide processing rather than ciliary transition-zone function. I am unaware of any human genetic study, functional assay, or animal model linking TCTN1 to deglycosylation defects, and the phenotypic overlap (developmental delay, hypotonia) is too nonspecific to constitute a biological rationale. A small residual probability is left for hypothesized links via general glycosylation effects on ciliary proteins or incidental co-mention in gene panels.

phenotype: craniofacial anomalies and anterior segment dysgenesis syndrome
justification: DNAJC13 (RME-8) is best known for endosomal trafficking and a candidate role in autosomal dominant Parkinson disease, but a distinct human syndrome of craniofacial anomalies with anterior segment dysgenesis has been attributed to heterozygous DNAJC13 variants in the clinical genetics literature (an OMIM-recognized phenotype), which implies at least one credible human report with de novo/segregating variants and supportive functional work on endosomal recycling relevant to ocular and craniofacial development. However, my recollection suggests the evidence base is small—likely one or a few probands/families rather than multiple independent replicating cohorts—so definitive "Established" status is uncertain. Supportive nonhuman data (zebrafish/mouse trafficking and eye development models) would only reinforce a hypothesized mechanism, not upgrade the human evidence. I therefore weight "Existing" most heavily, with meaningful probability on "Established" if additional independent probands have since been reported, and small residual probability that the association is only biologically inferred or spurious.

phenotype: gonadal dysgenesis, dysmorphic facies, retinal dystrophy, and myopathy
justification: MRAS is best known as a RAS/MAPK pathway gene with a well-established autosomal dominant role in Noonan syndrome with cardiac hypertrophy (NS11), which is supported by multiple human probands and functional work. I also recall an OMIM-listed, autosomal recessive entity "gonadal dysgenesis, dysmorphic facies, retinal dystrophy, and myopathy" (GDRM) attributed to biallelic MRAS variants, but my recollection is that this rests on a very small number of consanguineous families from a single or few reports, without broad independent replication. That level of evidence fits "Existing" best, with a moderate chance that additional families/functional confirmation have since elevated it toward "Established." Because RASopathy biology plausibly explains gonadal, craniofacial, retinal and muscle involvement, a residual weight goes to "Hypothesized." A smaller residual weight is retained for "Novel" in case my recollection of the specific gene assignment for GDRM is mistaken (other candidate genes such as MYRF have overlapping syndromic descriptions).
